bills.title: The Farm Laws
bills.kicker: Three Acts on how farm produce is sold, contracted and stored
bills.summary: Three laws let farmers sell outside government-regulated APMC mandis without state market fees, set up a framework for contract farming, and removed most stock limits on food staples. They began as ordinances in June 2020 and were passed in September. After a year of protests, Parliament repealed them in November 2021.
provisions: Trade outside APMC yards (farm gates, warehouses, cold storages and e-trading platforms) with no state market fee or cess.
Pre-sowing contracts between farmers and buyers for one season to five years, with the price stated up front. Disputes go to the SDM, with appeal to the Collector.
Cereals, pulses, oilseeds, onions and potatoes regulated only in extraordinary circumstances. Stock limits apply only after a 100% price rise (horticulture) or 50% (non-perishables).

votes.note: Passed 15 Sep (Essential Commodities) and 17 Sep (the other two). We found no recorded division count.
Passed by voice vote amid chaos. Opposition MPs say the Deputy Chairman refused their demand for a division (a recorded vote). The third bill passed on 22 Sep while most of the opposition boycotted.

committee.note: None of the three bills went to a parliamentary committee. Rajya Sabha did not adopt motions to send them to a Select Committee.

arguments_for.text: “One nation, one market”: farmers gain the freedom to sell to any buyer, anywhere, without mandi fees.
MSP and the mandi system will continue; the government offered a written assurance and said MSP procurement hit record levels.
Mandis are scarce: each one serves 496 sq km against a recommended 80 sq km, and 86% of landholdings are small or marginal. Competition could make APMCs more efficient.

arguments_against.text: Private buyers outside mandis have no duty to pay MSP. Farmers answered with “one nation, one MSP”.
Agriculture and markets are state subjects, so the Centre overrode the states.
Deregulation alone may not bring buyers: Bihar scrapped its APMC Act in 2006 and private investment did not follow.
The process was rushed: ordinances first, no committee scrutiny, and a voice vote in the Rajya Sabha.

timeline.text: Three ordinances promulgated during the COVID-19 lockdown.
Bills introduced in Lok Sabha.
Rajya Sabha passes two bills by voice vote; demand for a division refused.
Eight Rajya Sabha MPs suspended.
Laws gazetted after presidential assent.
“Delhi Chalo” march begins; farmers camp at Delhi’s borders for about a year.
Supreme Court stays all three laws and appoints an expert committee.
PM Modi announces repeal: “we couldn’t convince a section of farmers.”
Both Houses pass the Farm Laws Repeal Bill without debate.
Samyukt Kisan Morcha suspends the protest. It reports about 700 farmer deaths; the government says it has no record.
A new march for a legal MSP guarantee is stopped at the Punjab–Haryana border.

status.text: Repealed in November 2021. A legal guarantee for MSP, the farmers’ central demand, is still unresolved.

reflection.aye: You backed the reform. The laws passed, but they lasted 14 months: the Supreme Court suspended them and Parliament repealed them.
reflection.no: You voted against. In practice, the Rajya Sabha never counted the votes, so a “No” on 20 September was never recorded.
reflection.committee: You asked for a committee. That was the opposition’s demand on the floor, and it was refused. Even the RSS-affiliated Bharatiya Kisan Sangh wanted committee scrutiny.
reflection.abstain: You stayed out. Many opposition MPs walked out or boycotted on 22 September, and the third bill passed with almost no debate.

bills.question: Passed without a recorded vote, repealed without a debate. How much scrutiny should a law that affects millions of farmers get?

bills.title: Women’s Reservation
bills.kicker: The Constitution (106th Amendment) Act — Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam
bills.summary: Reserves one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha, state assemblies and the Delhi assembly for women, including within seats already reserved for SCs and STs. It applies only after the next census is published and constituencies are redrawn, and lasts 15 years unless Parliament extends it.
provisions: One-third of seats reserved for women in the Lok Sabha, state assemblies and the Delhi assembly.
One-third of SC/ST-reserved seats also reserved for women.
Takes effect only after the first census after commencement and the delimitation based on it.
Lasts 15 years, extendable by Parliament. Reserved seats rotate after each delimitation.

votes.note: Both Noes were AIMIM MPs. As a constitutional amendment it needed a two-thirds majority of members present and voting.

committee.note: The 2023 Bill went to no committee. Earlier versions did: a Joint Committee in 1996 and a Standing Committee in 2008.

arguments_for.text: It fulfils a demand pending since the 1996 Bill, with near-unanimous support across parties.

arguments_for.by: Jagdeep Dhankhar, then Rajya Sabha Chairman

arguments_for.text: Blocking the 2026 fast-track amendment denies women their quota.

arguments_against.text: Tying the quota to a census and delimitation delays a right indefinitely; it should apply immediately.
arguments_against.by: Petitioner Jaya Thakur (Congress leader), Supreme Court

arguments_against.text: Population-based delimitation would penalise southern states that controlled population growth, so the quota should be delinked from it.
The 2026 notification bringing the Act into force was “absolutely bizarre” in its timing.

timeline.text: Introduced as the first business in the new Parliament building.
Lok Sabha passes it, 454–2.
Rajya Sabha passes it, 214–0.
Gazetted after presidential assent.
Act brought into force, more than 900 days after passage — but still not operational.
A fast-track amendment to apply the quota in 2029 fails in Lok Sabha, 298–230. It needed 352.

status.text: In force since April 2026 but not yet operational: seats will be reserved only after the next census and delimitation.

reflection.aye: You joined 454 MPs. Almost everyone agreed on the goal; the fight was, and still is, over when it starts.
reflection.no: You joined 2 MPs. AIMIM’s two members were the only Noes in either House.
reflection.committee: You wanted scrutiny. The bill was introduced and passed within three days with no committee, though earlier versions had been examined twice.
reflection.abstain: You stayed out of a near-unanimous vote. Constitutional amendments are judged by members present and voting, so abstaining changes the threshold.

bills.question: Everyone voted yes, yet no woman has been elected to a reserved seat. Is a law passed if it hasn’t started?

bills.title: Citizenship Amendment
bills.summary: Fast-tracks Indian citizenship for Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi and Christian migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan who entered India on or before 31 December 2014. Muslims are not among the covered groups, which is the core of the controversy.
provisions: Six communities from three countries are no longer treated as “illegal migrants”.
Cut-off date: entry on or before 31 December 2014.
Residency needed for naturalisation cut to 5 years for these groups.
Sixth Schedule tribal areas of the North-East and Inner Line Permit areas are excluded.

votes.note: Introduced and passed the same day; the vote came around midnight.
A motion to send it to a Select Committee failed 92–113.

committee.note: The 2019 Bill went to no committee. Its 2016 predecessor was examined by a Joint Parliamentary Committee, then lapsed.

arguments_for.text: It gives refuge to religious minorities persecuted in neighbouring countries where Islam is the state religion.
“No Indian has anything to worry regarding this act” — it grants citizenship and takes none away.
It builds on a long-standing commitment to Partition-era minorities, and an earlier version was examined by a Joint Committee.

arguments_against.text: Granting citizenship by religion violates equality under Article 14 and secularism.
arguments_against.by: Indian Union Muslim League and other petitioners

arguments_against.text: Persecuted Muslim sects such as Ahmadis and Hazaras, and Tamils from Sri Lanka, are left out; combined with an NRC, it could leave Muslim citizens stateless.
It breaks the 1985 Assam Accord, which set a 1971 cut-off, and threatens Assam’s culture.

timeline.text: Introduced and passed in Lok Sabha, 311–80.
Rajya Sabha passes it, 125–105.
Presidential assent.
Act comes into force.
Rules notified, more than four years later.
First 14 citizenship certificates handed over.
Supreme Court listed final hearing of about 237–242 petitions for 5–12 May.

status.text: In force, with rules in use since March 2024. The constitutional challenge is before the Supreme Court; we found no verdict as of October 2026.

reflection.aye: You voted with the government. In the Rajya Sabha the margin was 20 votes — the closest of the four bills here.
reflection.no: You joined 105 Rajya Sabha members. Twenty more votes the other way would have tied it.
reflection.committee: You backed the Select Committee motion. It failed 92–113.
reflection.abstain: You stayed out. In a 125–105 vote, every abstention on one side mattered.

bills.question: Should a country’s citizenship law ever name religions? And who decides — Parliament or the courts?

bills.title: Data Protection
bills.kicker: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023
bills.summary: India’s first general law on digital personal data. Companies and government bodies must usually get clear consent before using your data, keep it safe and report breaches. You get rights to access, correct and erase it. The government can exempt its own agencies, and the Act narrows what the Right to Information Act can reveal about people.
provisions: Consent needed to process personal data, with some “legitimate uses” allowed without it.
Rights to access, correct and erase data, and to withdraw consent.
No tracking, behavioural monitoring or targeted ads aimed at children.
A Data Protection Board decides complaints and imposes penalties.
The government can exempt its agencies, and Section 44(3) amends the RTI Act’s personal-information exemption.

votes.note: Passed by voice vote; no division was recorded.
Passed by voice vote after the opposition walked out over Manipur.

committee.note: The 2023 Bill went to no committee. Its 2019 predecessor spent two years with a Joint Parliamentary Committee, then was withdrawn in August 2022.

arguments_for.text: India finally gets a data protection law with enforceable rights and a dedicated Board.
Replacing the sprawling 2019 bill with a leaner law was a “pragmatic move”.
Phased rules give businesses 12–18 months to build consent systems.

arguments_against.text: Section 44(3) guts the RTI Act by removing the public-interest override, blocking access to records like officials’ assets.
No exemption for journalism chills press freedom.
arguments_against.by: The Reporters Collective and other petitioners

arguments_against.text: Broad exemptions for government agencies risk an “Orwellian State”.

timeline.text: Government withdraws the 2019 Personal Data Protection Bill after the Joint Committee’s report.
New bill introduced in Lok Sabha.
Lok Sabha passes it by voice vote.
Rajya Sabha passes it by voice vote.
Presidential assent.
Rules notified in phases; the Data Protection Board starts at once.
Supreme Court issues notice on challenges and refers them to a larger bench, with no stay.

status.text: Partly in force. Consent-manager rules start in November 2026 and the core obligations in May 2027. Challenges are pending before a larger Supreme Court bench.

reflection.aye: You voted yes — but on a voice vote, nobody knows who did. No MP’s individual vote on this law was recorded.
reflection.no: You shouted “No”. On a voice vote the Chair judges which side is louder; unless someone demands a division, your vote leaves no record.
reflection.committee: You wanted a committee. The previous version spent two years with one and was then withdrawn; this one went straight to the floor.
reflection.abstain: You stayed out — as much of the opposition did, having walked out over Manipur.

bills.question: A law on your personal data passed without a single recorded vote. Should major laws always require a division?

bills.title: A Uniform Civil Code
bills.kicker: The bill Parliament has never been asked to pass
bills.summary: A Uniform Civil Code would replace the separate Hindu, Muslim, Christian and Parsi personal laws on marriage, divorce, inheritance and adoption with one law for everyone. The Constitution has directed the state to “endeavour to secure” it since 1950. In seventy-six years no government has introduced one in Parliament — so this is the one bill here you cannot look up. Four states have passed their own.
provisions: One law on marriage, divorce, maintenance, inheritance and adoption, applying regardless of religion.

Replaces the Hindu Marriage Act 1955, the Hindu Succession Act 1956, the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937, the Indian Christian Marriage Act 1872 and the Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act 1936.
The Special Marriage Act 1954 already offers a religion-neutral marriage to anyone who opts in; a UCC would make it the default rather than a choice.
Every state code passed so far exempts Scheduled Tribes.

votes.note: No government has ever introduced a national Uniform Civil Code bill in either House. A private member's bill was introduced in the Rajya Sabha in December 2022 — the motion merely to introduce it carried 63–23 and the bill went no further.

The nearest real vote. Passed by voice vote; the opposition's demand to send it to a select committee was rejected. Reports do not break the voice vote down by party, so no party's MLAs can be said to have voted either way.

committee.note: The 21st Law Commission examined it and reported in 2018. The 22nd reopened consultation in June 2023, received about 46 lakh responses, and its term lapsed in August 2024 without it producing a UCC report.

arguments_for.text: The Constitution already directs it: “The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.”
arguments_for.by: Article 44, Directive Principles of State Policy

arguments_for.text: Personal laws are where women lose most. A Muslim women's organisation found that about 90% of the 4,700 women it surveyed wanted polygamy ended — a reform their own personal law blocks.
arguments_for.by: Zakia Soman, Bharatiya Muslim Mahila Andolan

arguments_for.text: One rule for inheritance and divorce is simpler to administer than five, and Uttarakhand's experience suggests the machinery can cope: about 4.7 lakh marriages were registered in its first year, nearly all online.

arguments_against.text: Even its architect did not want it forced on everyone at the start. Ambedkar told the Constituent Assembly the article “does not require enforcement on all citizens merely because they are citizens”, and suggested Parliament might begin by making the code purely voluntary.

The government's own law reform body examined it and said no: a uniform civil code is “neither necessary nor desirable at this stage”. It recommended fixing the discriminatory parts of each personal law instead.
arguments_against.by: 21st Law Commission of India, consultation paper, 2018

arguments_against.text: Equal rights need not mean an identical law. The demand should be “uniformity of rights, not a uniform law” — and historically it was Hindu law, not minority law, that was the most gender-unjust.
arguments_against.by: Flavia Agnes, lawyer and women's rights scholar

arguments_against.text: Several of the governing coalition's own allies reject it. Mizoram's assembly passed a resolution against a UCC in February 2023, and parties in Nagaland and Meghalaya have opposed it as a threat to customary law.
arguments_against.by: MNF, NDPP, NPF and NPP — all NDA allies

timeline.text: The Constituent Assembly debates it. Amendments by four Muslim members to protect personal law are defeated; Ambedkar suggests the code could begin as voluntary.
Article 44 comes into force as a Directive Principle — a goal the state must work towards, but which no court can enforce.
In the Shah Bano case the Supreme Court regrets that Article 44 “has remained a dead letter”. Parliament responds by passing a law reversing the judgment.
The 21st Law Commission concludes a UCC is “neither necessary nor desirable at this stage”.
The 22nd Law Commission reopens consultation and receives about 46 lakh responses. Its term lapses in August 2024 without a report.
Uttarakhand becomes the first state to pass a UCC, by voice vote.
The Uttarakhand code comes into force.
Gujarat passes its own UCC. Assam follows in May and Madhya Pradesh in July.
Amit Shah says every NDA-ruled state will have a UCC before 2029. Still no bill in Parliament.

status.text: No national UCC bill exists. Four states have passed their own and more have announced them, so the country is getting a patchwork of civil codes rather than a uniform one — which is close to the opposite of what Article 44 describes.

reflection.aye: You voted for it — so look at what the states that did this actually got. Uttarakhand registered about 4.7 lakh marriages in its first year, so the administration coped. But its most argued-over provision, registering live-in relationships, was used 68 times in twelve months. And every state code so far exempts Scheduled Tribes, so none of them is fully uniform.
reflection.no: You voted against — and so, in effect, has every government since 1950. None has introduced a bill. The Law Commission reached your conclusion in 2018 and proposed the alternative: fix the unjust parts of each personal law one at a time, which is how triple talaq was ended in 2019.
reflection.committee: You asked for scrutiny. That has been tried twice. The 21st Law Commission reported in 2018 and said no. The 22nd reopened the question in 2023, collected about 46 lakh responses, and its term ran out before it wrote anything. Referral is not always a delaying tactic — but it is not always an answer either.
reflection.abstain: You abstained on the one bill here that was never put to a vote. That is roughly what Parliament has done for seventy-six years: Article 44 says the state “shall endeavour”, and endeavouring has meant leaving it to the states.

bills.question: The Constitution asks for one civil code. Four states have now written four different ones. Is that progress towards Article 44, or away from it?

bills.title: The Income Tax Rewrite
bills.kicker: The Income-tax Act, 2025 — replacing the law of 1961
bills.summary: The first full rewrite of India's income tax law in sixty-four years. It was meant to be simpler: shorter sections, plain tables, and one “tax year” in place of the confusing “previous year” and “assessment year”. It also wrote into law the tax officer's power to break into your email, cloud storage and social media during a search. The Lok Sabha passed it in about three minutes, without debate.
provisions: Replaces the Income-tax Act 1961 in full, from 1 April 2026.
Cuts length and jargon: formulae and tables replace long provisos, and a single “tax year” replaces “previous year” and “assessment year”.
Mostly a redraft, not a tax cut — the ₹12 lakh rebate and the new slabs came from the Finance Act 2025, a separate law.
Section 247 lets authorised officers override access codes to search a “computer system” during a raid; section 261 defines that to include email, cloud, online investment accounts and social media.

votes.note: Introduced and passed the same day by voice vote, reportedly in about three minutes, with no debate, while the opposition protested over the revision of Bihar's electoral rolls.
Returned to the Lok Sabha by voice vote the next day. As a Money Bill, the Rajya Sabha could recommend changes but not block it.

committee.note: The February 2025 version did go to a Select Committee under Baijayant Panda, which made more than 285 recommendations and reported in July 2025. The government then withdrew that bill and introduced a fresh one, which passed the same day it was introduced — so the bill that became law was never itself examined by a committee.

arguments_for.text: The 1961 Act had been amended so many times it had become unreadable. The rewrite cuts the word count roughly in half and replaces tangled provisos with tables and formulae.
A single “tax year” removes a genuine and long-standing source of confusion for ordinary taxpayers filing returns.
arguments_for.by: Select Committee on the Income-tax Bill, chaired by Baijayant Panda

arguments_for.text: The Select Committee's scrutiny was real: it made more than 285 recommendations, and the government accepted enough of them to withdraw its own bill and start again.

arguments_against.text: A law governing every taxpayer in the country passed in roughly three minutes with no debate, after the version a committee had actually examined was withdrawn.
The power to compel access to a person's email, cloud storage and social media during a search is far broader than a search of premises, and may not survive constitutional scrutiny.
arguments_against.by: Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, pre-Budget memorandum, January 2026

arguments_against.text: Commentary claiming the digital search power was dropped from the final Act is wrong: the phrase moved, but section 261's definition of “computer system” carries the same reach.

timeline.text: The Income-tax Bill 2025 is introduced in the Lok Sabha and sent to a Select Committee.
The Select Committee reports, with more than 285 recommendations.
The government withdraws that bill.
A fresh bill is introduced and passed by the Lok Sabha the same day, by voice vote, in about three minutes.
The Rajya Sabha returns it by voice vote.
Presidential assent.
The Supreme Court hears a petition against the digital search power and declines to entertain it, unpersuaded that the power is unguided.
The Act comes into force, replacing the 1961 law.

status.text: In force since 1 April 2026. The constitutional challenge to the digital search power was refused a hearing in February 2026, so section 247 stands.

reflection.aye: You voted for it. So did the House — though on a voice vote nobody's name is recorded, so there is no way to show that you did. Most of what you approved was a redraft; the part that was genuinely new was the digital search power, and it was not debated.
reflection.no: You voted against. On a voice vote the Chair judges which side sounded louder, and unless a member demands a division, no count is taken. The record of this law shows no opponents at all.
reflection.committee: You asked for a committee — and this is the one bill here that got one. The Select Committee made over 285 recommendations. Then the government withdrew that bill and passed a new one the day it was introduced. The law in force was never examined by a committee in its final form.
reflection.abstain: You stayed out. Much of the opposition effectively did too: they were protesting about Bihar's electoral rolls while the tax law went through in about three minutes.

bills.question: A committee spent five months on this bill. The version that became law was passed in three minutes. What was the committee for?
